summary: Describes architecture and protocol requirements for controlling a Media Gateway from a Media Gateway Controller, the split used to connect telephone networks with Internet voice systems. It lays out what such a control protocol needs to do. It is an informational memo.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2805 describes what a control protocol between a Media Gateway Controller and a Media Gateway needs to support. It covers call setup, media handling, gateway resources, reliability and security rather than defining message rules.

questions: what is a media gateway controller
what does a media gateway controller do
what must a media gateway control protocol support
subtitle: Requirements for a controller to manage media gateways across telephone and packet networks.

tldr.problem: Media gateways translate between network types, but a separate controller needs a consistent way to control calls and gateway resources across different implementations.
tldr.mechanism: The memo lists requirements for the Media Gateway Control Protocol, covering calls, resources, operations, transport, security and specific bearer and application types. It does not define the protocol itself.
tldr.outcome: The requirements cover gateways from small devices to large systems and name Megaco/H.248 as the protocol context. RFC 2805 is Informational.

sections.title: The Gateway and Its Controller
sections.content:
A Media Gateway (MG) maps or converts media between networks, such as a circuit-switched telephone network and a packet network. A Media Gateway Controller (MGC) controls an MG. A termination is a point where media enters or leaves the gateway, and a connection associates two or more terminations.

The memo sets requirements for a Media Gateway Control Protocol between the MGC and MG. It assumes the gateway may be built in different ways, so the same controller request should produce the same function across implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: The gateway converts media. The controller tells it which connections and media tasks to handle, without needing to know the gateway's internal design.

sections.title: Calls, Media and Resource Control
sections.content:
The protocol must support reserving and releasing resources, connecting circuit and packet terminations, changing connections during a call, and handling one-way or two-way media flows. It must also let the controller request media transformations such as echo cancellation and control how tones and detected events are handled.

The gateway must report resource status and support discovery so the controller can learn which resources and settings are available. The controller may name an exact resource or let the gateway choose from a requested set.
sections.plainLanguage: The controller needs to reserve lines, connect call participants, request media changes and learn when resources change. The gateway reports what it can provide.

sections.title: Reliability, Transport and Security
sections.content:
The protocol must help the controller and gateway detect loss of contact and mismatches in their view of connections or resources. It must allow backup controllers, orderly recovery and continued support for connections already established when a controller fails.

The underlying network may lose, reorder or duplicate messages. The protocol must correlate commands and responses, report command failures and prevent loss of one packet from blocking unrelated messages. Security requirements include mutual authentication, protection of control messages and optional confidentiality.
sections.plainLanguage: Messages can be lost or repeated, so both sides need ways to detect problems and recover. They also need to verify who is sending control commands.

sections.title: Scale and Timing Expectations
sections.content:
The requirements cover MGs ranging from one termination to millions, and MGCs controlling from one MG to a few tens of thousands. The protocol should minimize message exchanges and allow capability discovery and independent version upgrades.

For continuity testing, the memo specifies a maximum 200 ms delay for cross-MGC Initial Address Message propagation and a maximum 200 ms from the end of dialing to that message's emission. It also says the architecture should not rule out peak calling rates on the order of 140 calls per second on a moderately loaded network.
sections.plainLanguage: The requirements include both small and very large gateways. They also set timing targets for call signaling and expect the protocol not to limit a stated peak call rate.

sections.title: Bearer Types and Applications
sections.content:
The protocol must support different bearer types, including circuit, packet and ATM connections. Application-specific requirements cover trunking and access gateways, fax, text telephones, Network Access Servers, multimedia gateways and audio resources.

The Audio Resource Function requirements include playing announcements, collecting touch-tone digits, recording audio, speech recognition and conferencing. The controller needs to specify and control these functions through a common protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: Gateways may handle phone lines, packet media, fax, text, modems or conference calls. The protocol must describe these different jobs in a way the controller can request.
